name: AROS Research Operating System
summary: Free, portable and lightweight operating system reimplementing the programming interfaces and preemptive multitasking of AmigaOS 3.1 on modern architectures.
license: Open Source (AROS Public License - APL, derived from the Mozilla Public License 1.1)

content.introduction: AROS Research Operating System (initially named Amiga Research OS, renamed AROS for trademark reasons) is an international free and open-source operating system project started in 1995. Faced with the financial collapse of Commodore and the risk of extinction of the Amiga platform, AROS was designed to reimplement cleanly, independently and portably the whole set of system libraries and programming interfaces (APIs) of AmigaOS 3.1 (published in 1994) on modern hardware architectures and microprocessors.
content.what_is_it: Technically, AROS is neither a Linux distribution nor a derivative of Unix or Windows: it is a stand-alone system designed from scratch to revive the engineering philosophy of AmigaOS. Its modular architecture is organised around Exec, a real-time preemptive multitasking microkernel managing task scheduling with priorities, hardware interrupts and message lists. As on the classic Amiga, AROS adopts by default a flat memory model without hardware protection between processes, which gives it almost instantaneous context switches and exceptional responsiveness, while requiring absolute rigour from software to avoid memory corruption.
content.core_subsystems_intuition_and_graphics: Above Exec, AROS reimplements the emblematic libraries of the Amiga system: Intuition (the windowing and graphical interface manager), Graphics (2D matrix and vector drawing engine, supporting hardware 3D acceleration through Gallium3D/Mesa on certain compatible graphics chipsets) and AmigaDOS (management of input/output streams and file systems). The default user interface is the Wanderer graphical desktop (modern clone of the AmigaOS Workbench). The toolkit for building interfaces is Zune, an object-oriented implementation fully API-compatible with the MUI (Magic User Interface) library.
content.native_vs_hosted_modes_and_ports: AROS stands out for its great versatility in its execution methods: it exists in two main forms, AROS Native and AROS Hosted. In Native mode, AROS boots directly on bare metal as the main operating system, available for 32-bit x86 (IA-32), x86-64, ARM (Raspberry Pi boards) and PowerPC (Sam440, Efika boards). In Hosted mode, AROS runs as a windowed process on top of an existing host operating system (Linux, FreeBSD, macOS or Windows), offering an ideal environment for application development and debugging.
content.amiga_compatibility_source_vs_binary: A rigorous distinction must be made between source-level compatibility and binary compatibility. On the x86 or ARM architecture, AROS offers API compatibility (source-compatible): software written in the C language for AmigaOS 3.1 can be recompiled and work natively. To run the historical Amiga software and video games compiled for the Motorola 680x0 (m68k) processor, AROS Native includes transparent emulation mechanisms (notably through the Janus-UAE subsystem). On the dedicated AROS m68k port (designed for real classic Amiga computers and FPGA accelerator boards such as the Vampire), on the other hand, binary compatibility with m68k code is direct and native.
content.filesystems_hardware_support_and_limitat: AROS supports reading and writing the historical Amiga file systems (OFS, FFS, SFS) as well as the contemporary FAT12/16/32, ISO 9660 and ext2/ext3 formats. While it runs directly on compatible PCs and hypervisors (QEMU, VirtualBox, VMware), AROS remains an enthusiast system subject to hardware limitations: support for recent Wi-Fi chips, Bluetooth and advanced power management (ACPI) remains partial. The system is distributed under the free AROS Public License (APL), derived from the Mozilla Public License (MPL 1.1), and its development is publicly hosted on GitHub.
content.history_and_project_goals: The first discussions reported by the project go back to 1993, when Amiga users were looking for an answer to Commodore's difficulties; the team dates the project to 1995, the year retained in the site copyright notice. The original name, Amiga Research Operating System, was dropped in favour of the acronym AROS for trademark reasons. The published goals are compatibility with AmigaOS 3.1, portability to x86, PowerPC, Alpha, Sparc and HPPA, binary compatibility on Amiga and source compatibility on the other architectures, with two execution modes: native on the hardware or hosted in a window of the host system. The site sums up the approach with an explicit comparison: API-level compatibility, "like Wine, unlike UAE".
content.ports_and_hosted_flavors: AROS ports follow the platform-processor nomenclature. The project distinguishes two flavours: native ports boot directly on the hardware and take control of it; hosted ports run on top of an existing system, without direct access to the hardware, which avoids writing low-level drivers and allows development without rebooting the machine. The official ports page lists amiga-m68k, pc-i386, pc-x86_64, pc-x86_64-smp, linux-i386 and linux-x86-64, mingw32-i386, darwin-i386, darwin-x86-64, darwin-ppc, raspi-armhf and sam440-ppc. The GitHub repository adds builds for raspi-aarch64, raspi-aarch64-smp, opensbi-riscv64, linux-arm and linux-armhf.
content.build_channels_and_toolchains: The download page offers no numbered stable version: it refers to nightly builds and snapshots, with a warning stating that these builds are intended for developers and testers, that they are not always stable and that they lack most of the applications of everyday use. The GitHub repository describes the build chain employed: GCC 6.5.0 as the reference configuration, more recent versions (9.5.0, 10.5.0, 13.5.0, 15.2.0, 16.2.0) and LLVM builds (11.0.0, 20.1.0, 23.1.0), produced by an Azure Pipelines chain hosted in the repository.
content.documentation_structure: The official documentation is divided into separate manuals: introduction, progress status, ports, licence, download, installation, use of the shell, applications, FAQ, hardware compatibility and glossary. The installation guide details the procedures per flavour, up to booting through GRUB, and opens with a maturity warning: AROS is described there as alpha-quality software, intended for experimentation and development rather than for finished use. The code is hosted on GitHub in the aros-development-team/AROS repository, and the site maintains a Contact page and a Developers page as entry points.
content.licensing_terms: The code is distributed under AROS Public License (APL) version 1.1, whose official text presents itself as "based on the MPL". The licence defines commercial use as the distribution of the covered code to a third party and frames the rights granted over the original code, the modifications and the patents. It covers the code; the trademarks cited on the site remain the property of their holders, the legal notice specifying that Amiga is a trademark of Amiga Inc. and that the other trademarks belong to their respective owners.
advantages: Free, modern and open-source reimplementation of the programming interfaces and the spirit of AmigaOS 3.1.
Ultra-responsive preemptive multitasking and almost instant boot on contemporary microprocessors.
Great portability thanks to the Native (bare metal) and Hosted (on top of Linux, macOS or Windows) execution modes.
Wanderer graphical desktop and Zune toolkit compatible with the MUI interfaces of AmigaOS.
Built-in transparent m68k emulation (Janus-UAE) making it possible to launch historical Amiga software and games.
Open source code governed by the free AROS Public License (APL).
disadvantages: Absence by default of hardware memory protection between processes (an application crash can freeze the system).
Restricted modern hardware support on recent physical computers (Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, recent 3D GPUs).
m68k binary compatibility on x86 requires an intermediate software emulation (Janus-UAE).
Application ecosystem mainly oriented towards retrogaming and heritage preservation.
Not suited to a secure multi-user server environment or to modern enterprise office work.
who_is_it_for: Nostalgic users, enthusiasts and developers of the Amiga ecosystem wishing to keep the spirit of AmigaOS alive.
Developers curious to experiment with preemptive multitasking system programming without heavy abstraction.
Amiga emulation and retrogaming enthusiasts using ready-to-use distributions such as Icaros Desktop.
Virtualisation enthusiasts exploring alternative operating systems under QEMU or VirtualBox.
who_is_it_not_for: General public users looking for a primary system for modern office work or complex web browsing.
Enterprises and data centres requiring strict multi-user environments with access rights management.
Modern video game players requiring recent Vulkan or DirectX graphics drivers.
Developers depending on modern containerisation tools (Docker, Kubernetes).
content.verdict: AROS Research Operating System is a free reimplementation of AmigaOS 3.1: it reproduces its APIs and its preemptive multitasking architecture on modern hardware architectures, which maintains the Amiga software heritage independently of the original proprietary hardware.
content.installation_media_and_boot_targets: The official installation guide recommends the CD-ROM as the boot medium and describes installation on hard disk as the main target, either as a single system or alongside another system already installed (Windows, Linux or other). A boot floppy remains documented as a boot medium. The minimum configuration indicated is a PC-AT with a PCI bus equipped with an i486 or higher processor, 24 MB of RAM, a PS/2, AT or USB keyboard and, preferably, a VESA graphics card. The boot images were converted with grub-mkrescue in order to boot both on machines with BIOS firmware and on those with EFI firmware.
content.firewall_and_security_hardening: The activity report published by the project on 29 July 2026 lists the security work of the past year: a systematic hardening pass of memory safety and security across the whole network stack, the addition of a Roadshow-compatible firewall (ipf/ipnat) with a dedicated Firewall graphical interface, support for SYN cookies and for the randomisation of initial sequence numbers in the TCP stack, as well as a cryptographic random number generator backed by entropy.resource. The same report mentions the hardening of the NTFS manager and the correction of edge cases in the memory allocator.
